idiom_name: duck typing + module as contract documentation
implementation_notes: Ruby has no interface type: the contract is the set of messages the collaborator answers and any object that responds can be injected, so the separated interface exists only as convention - documented by a module, often with a method that raises NotImplementedError, and enforced by a shared contract test suite. Keep the module-of-stubs form when you want a clear failure message; otherwise rely on duck typing and run the same tests against every implementation.
code_sketch:
module Clock
  def now
    raise NotImplementedError, "#{self.class} must implement #now"
  end
end
class SystemClock
  include Clock
  def now = Time.now.to_f
end
class Report
  def initialize(clock) = @clock = clock   # any #now responder
end
pitfalls: No compile-time conformance: a collaborator missing #now raises NoMethodError only at the call site.
method_missing-based collaborators answer respond_to? incorrectly unless respond_to_missing? is also defined.
Monkey patches and refinements can change an injected class's behaviour underneath the contract.
